analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover and renew people with preexisting conditions who change or lose jobs.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate's Democratic leader with zero cosponsors, the bill sat on the Senate calendar for more than eight months and died without ever coming to a vote when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred health insurers from refusing to cover a whole group or to renew a policy, and would have required them to sell individual coverage — at any premium state law allows — to people leaving group coverage, while capping preexisting-condition exclusions at 12 months with credit for prior coverage. It also added a mental health parity rule, a gradually larger tax deduction for self-employed people's health insurance, penalty-free IRA withdrawals for catastrophic medical bills and for laid-off workers' premiums, purchasing cooperatives so small employers and individuals could pool their buying power, and a new federal health care fraud enforcement program. It was paid for partly with new taxes on wealthy Americans who give up U.S. citizenship and by ending deductions for company-owned life insurance. None of it was ever debated or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families who change or lose jobs and would otherwise be locked out of coverage because of a health condition; people with preexisting conditions, whose exclusion periods would be capped at 12 months and reduced month-for-month by prior coverage, with pregnancy, birth, and adoption carved out entirely; people with mental illness, whose plans could no longer impose treatment limits or cost-sharing on mental health care that they do not impose on other conditions; self-employed people, whose health insurance deduction would rise from 30% of costs to 80% by 2006; unemployed people, who could withdraw from IRAs without penalty to pay premiums; small employers and individuals, who could form certified purchasing cooperatives to bargain for coverage; and Medicare and Medicaid, backed by a new coordinated fraud-and-abuse enforcement program with mandatory exclusion of felons and new federal fraud crimes.

how_it_helps.text: Insurers could no longer decline to offer coverage to an entire group, and premiums and eligibility rules could not be based on health status, medical history, genetic information, or disability.
People who had at least 18 months of group coverage and could not rejoin a group plan were guaranteed the right to buy an individual policy with no denial or exclusion based on their health.

Preexisting-condition exclusions would be capped at 12 months (18 for late enrollees) and reduced one month for each month of prior qualifying coverage, with no exclusion at all for pregnancy or for a child's first 12 months after birth or adoption.
Health plans could not impose treatment limits or financial requirements on mental health services that are stricter than what they impose for other conditions.

Self-employed individuals' health insurance costs would become 80% deductible by 2006, up from 30%, and IRA withdrawals would be penalty-free for financially devastating medical expenses and for premiums while unemployed.
States would have to certify health plan purchasing cooperatives so small employers and individuals could join together to compare and buy coverage, with an ombudsman for enrollees.

A new federal fraud-and-abuse control program would coordinate enforcement, pay tipsters a share of recoveries, mandatorily exclude from Medicare anyone convicted of a health care fraud felony, and create new federal health care fraud crimes.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans bear the new coverage obligations: they must sell and renew without health screening, credit prior coverage, and follow disclosure rules, though premium-setting stays with them. Wealthy expatriates — those averaging more than $100,000 in annual income tax or worth $500,000 or more — would face tax on their assets as if sold on the day they gave up citizenship, with $600,000 excluded. Life insurers would lose the deduction for interest on loans tied to company-owned insurance and annuity contracts, and thrift savings associations would lose the bad-debt reserve tax method. Health care providers face expanded fraud enforcement, higher civil penalties, and new criminal exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and wealthy tax avoiders

drawbacks.text: The guaranteed-issue rules deliberately leave premiums untouched: the bill states that nothing affects an insurer's determination of the premium amount, so an insurer could accept an applicant with a preexisting condition and still charge a rate that makes the coverage unaffordable in practice.

Protections stop well short of banning exclusions: insurers could still exclude treatment of a preexisting condition for up to 12 months, and anyone with a lapse in coverage longer than 30 days gets no credit at all for prior coverage.

The bill carves managed care plans out of anti-kickback penalties for risk-sharing arrangements with providers under written agreements, and its committee statement urges tax incentives for medical savings accounts — provisions that reduce pressure on the industry and shift more cost onto patients through high deductibles.

Letting HMOs offer high-deductible plans paired with medical savings accounts means participants pay routine care out of their own accounts, which helps higher earners who can fund the account while exposing lower-income members to deductibles they may not be able to pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and were the most valuable kind in 1996 — keeping coverage when a job ends is often the difference between treatment and no treatment. But the design is incomplete: guaranteeing that an insurer must sell without limiting what it can charge can make coverage a right on paper only, and the 30-day coverage lapse trap plus the 12-month exclusion window still leaves many sick people exposed. The managed-care safe harbor and medical-savings-account push tilt the bill toward the industry in places. On balance the bill favors working people's interests, but the affordability gap and partial carve-outs are serious flaws an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Democratic leader introduced it, the Senate read it twice and placed it straight on the legislative calendar without any committee consideration, and nobody ever brought it up for a vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle of South Dakota, the Senate's Democratic leader, introduced the bill on April 24, 1996, and not a single senator — from either party — signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill skipped the committee process entirely: it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 379) on April 25, 1996, and no committee ever held a hearing or markup on it.

After that, the record shows no further action of any kind — no floor debate, no amendments, no roll-call vote — leaving the bill to die on the calendar when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, especially in the individual market, were better off because the bill never advanced: they kept the ability to turn applicants down, refuse to renew, and price coverage based on health, free of any federal floor. Workers with preexisting conditions got nothing from this bill, since it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers in the individual market

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it read twice and placed directly on the Senate calendar, bypassing committee referral

against.name: Bob Dole, then Trent Lott
against.role: Senate Majority Leaders during the bill's lifespan
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for floor action; it sat on the Senate calendar from April 25, 1996 until the Congress ended with no vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no partisan split — only that the bill sat untouched on the calendar for over eight months.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to offer and renew coverage without health-based screening and to limit preexisting-condition exclusions, but it leaves premium-setting entirely to them and state law — so coverage could be guaranteed in name yet priced out of reach. Insurers' core interest here, preserving medical underwriting and free premium setting, runs against what sick people need from the bill.

The bill lets HMOs offer high-deductible plans to members with medical savings accounts and exempts written risk-sharing arrangements with providers from anti-kickback penalties, expanding what managed care can do. It also subjects Medicare HMOs to intermediate sanctions for the first time.

Expanded fraud enforcement, mandatory Medicare exclusion for anyone convicted of a health care or drug felony, higher civil monetary penalties, and new federal fraud and embezzlement crimes all increase providers' legal exposure. Their interest in avoiding enforcement runs against patients and taxpayers.

The bill denies the tax deduction for interest on loans with respect to company-owned life insurance, endowment, and annuity contracts, closing a corporate financing technique and using the revenue to help pay for the health provisions.

Qualified long-term care contracts would get federal tax treatment as medical care and as non-taxable benefits, creating a tax-favored product market, while the same title imposes consumer-protection standards on the policies.

Expatriates with over $100,000 in average annual income tax or a net worth of $500,000 or more would owe tax as if their property were sold on the day they left, closing the door on renouncing citizenship to escape U.S. taxes.
